spoken: Budapest, the 16th of June, 1989. On the steps of an art hall on Heroes' Square lie six coffins.
Four hold men executed after 1956, and one a man who died in prison.
The sixth is empty, for all the dead.
Some 200,000 to 250,000 people have come, 31 years to the day since Im-reh Nodge, prime minister in 1956, was executed.
How did Hungary get from a secret execution to this? This is what 1956 left behind.
By December 1956 the revolution was crushed, and Yah-nosh Kah-dahr, put in power by the Soviet army, governed Hungary.
In December came the summary courts. A hidden weapon now meant at least ten years in prison.
Anyone seen as a danger could be interned, held without trial for months.
By the 1956 Institute's count, courts jailed more than 22,000 people, and even more were held without trial.
In all, about one Hungarian in two hundred lost their liberty.
And 229 people were executed for their part in the revolution. Most had fought in it.
Even by the regime's own figures, at most 5 in 100 were class enemies. Most were workers, peasants, clerks and students.
Internment ended in 1961, and most prisoners went free only in 1963.
Many did not wait. On the 28th of October, Austria had offered asylum to any Hungarian who asked.
After the 4th of November, people set out west in their tens of thousands.
Near the Austrian village of Ahn-dow, a narrow wooden bridge crossed the Ein-zer canal, close to the border.
From the 6th of November, about 70,000 people crossed it, by Austrian accounts.
On the 21st of November the bridge was blown up. People still crossed over its ruins.
In December, as the reprisals began, a second, larger wave left.
Hungary's statistics office counted 193,885 people who fled, most of them to Austria.
Nearly two in three were men, and seven in ten were aged 15 to 39.
About 10,000 children under 15 left without their parents. And one in ten of Hungary's engineers left.
The UN's refugee agency coordinated relief. The United States took some 44,000 people, and Canada some 39,000.
Only 11,447 had come home by the end of May 1957. About 176,000 stayed abroad for good.
Im-reh Nodge, prime minister during the revolution, had taken refuge in the Yugoslav embassy on the 4th of November.
Pahl Mah-lay-tair, his defence minister, had been arrested the night before, at talks with the Soviet army.
Kah-dahr's government promised in writing that they could go home. On the 22nd of November, they boarded a bus.
Soviet soldiers boarded too, armoured cars escorted the bus away, and the group was taken to Romania.
In early 1957, Kah-dahr's party leaders, with Moscow's agreement, decided to put them on trial.
The trial opened in February 1958, was halted at Moscow's request, and resumed in June behind closed doors.
The historian Yah-nosh Rye-ner concludes that the decisive, though not the only, responsibility was Kah-dahr's.
On the 15th of June, 1958, the court sentenced Nodge, Mah-lay-tair, and the journalist Mick-lohsh Ghee-mesh, to death.
Others got prison terms. Gay-zah Lo-shon-tsee had died in custody, and Yo-zhef See-lah-djee had been executed in April.
Nodge did not ask for mercy. I do not ask for clemency, he told the court.
They were hanged at dawn on the 16th of June in a Budapest prison yard, and buried there without a mark.
Only then was the trial made public.
In 1961 their coffins were moved in secret to plot three oh one of a Budapest cemetery, among many executed after 1956, under false names.
Kah-dahr led the ruling party until 1988, and was twice prime minister.
In 1961 he offered a bargain. Whoever is not against us, he said, is with us.
In 1962, after a secret understanding with Washington, the UN dropped the Hungarian question from its agenda.
In March 1963 came an amnesty. Most of those jailed for 1956 went free; several hundred stayed in prison.
From 1968 a reform brought some market rules into the planned economy.
By official figures, real wages rose by half from 1960 to 1975, then stalled, and fell in the 1980s.
Some called it goulash communism, a softer dictatorship, but a dictatorship still.
The other side of the bargain was silence. In school books, 1956 was a counter-revolution.
By the 1980s it had softened to the regrettable events, but public commemoration was still forbidden.
In May 1988, as the regime weakened, Kah-dahr was replaced as party leader.
Former prisoners of 1956 founded a Committee for Historical Justice, and demanded the rehabilitation of the executed.
On the 16th of June, 1988, people gathered at the nameless graves. In the city, police beat demonstrators.
Then, on the 28th of January, 1989, a minister, Im-reh Pozh-guy, called 1956 a popular uprising.
That spring, the graves in plot three oh one were opened, and Nodge and his companions identified.
On the 16th of June, 1989, came the funeral we began with, broadcast live on radio and television.
Speakers called for the Soviet troops to leave, and for free elections.
Speaking for the young, Viktor Or-bahn said that democracy and communism are incompatible.
At the cemetery the names of the executed were read out, and the dead were buried again, with their names.
On the 6th of July the Supreme Court annulled the verdict of 1958. That same day, Kah-dahr died.
On the 23rd of October, 1989, exactly 33 years after the revolution began, the People's Republic became the Republic of Hungary.
The acting head of state, Mah-chahsh Sue-rush, proclaimed it from the balcony of Parliament, before tens of thousands.
In 1990 came free elections, and a new law made the 23rd of October a national day.
On the 19th of June, 1991, the last Soviet soldier left Hungary.
The students' first demand in 1956 had been that Soviet troops leave. It took 35 years.
Today, on the 23rd of October, flags with a hole fly again, as they did in 1956.
Plot three oh one is now a national memorial park, and the bridge at Ahn-dow was rebuilt in 1996.
1956 left many dead. There were fighters and bystanders, Hungarian and Soviet soldiers, victims of the secret police, and secret policemen lynched by crowds.
It left some 200,000 lives begun again abroad, and three decades of silence at home.
And it left names. For thirty years they were kept off the graves. Now they are back, and remembered.
